title: Humboldt's America
subtitle: Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland in Spanish America and the United States, 1799–1804
intro: On 5 June 1799 a Spanish mail ship left A Coruña with a Prussian mining official turned naturalist, Alexander von Humboldt, and a French botanist, Aimé Bonpland, aboard. They carried an unusual royal licence from Carlos IV that let two foreigners roam Spain's American empire with barometers, chronometers and plant presses. For five years they crossed what are now Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Mexico, and ended with a few crowded weeks in Philadelphia and Washington as Thomas Jefferson's guests. Humboldt's books later reshaped how Europeans pictured the Americas and how scientists thought about nature as one connected system.

This chapter tries to look at that journey from more than one side. Humboldt's own record is huge: the bound field diaries (the Amerikanische Reisetagebücher, bought for the Berlin State Library in 2013 and now digitised) and dozens of dated letters, above all to his brother Wilhelm. Next to them sit the voices of the people he met. Francisco José de Caldas, a self-taught creole astronomer from Popayán, wrote dated letters full of delight and then hurt. José Celestino Mutis ran the royal botanical expedition in Bogotá. Viceroy Pedro Mendinueta sent a confidential warning to Madrid, and a Spanish naval commander filled his log with suspicion. In the United States, Jefferson wrote letters, Charles Willson Peale kept a diary and Albert Gallatin wrote to his wife.

The heart of the chapter is a single night. In the small hours of 12 November 1799 the Leonid meteors came down as a storm. Humboldt and Bonpland watched from Cumaná. The American surveyor Andrew Ellicott watched from a ship in the Florida Keys, and Moravian missionaries in Labrador recorded the terror of an Inuit man named Kapik. Months later, deep in the Orinoco missions, Humboldt found that Spanish friars had written the same night into their parish books. One sky, written down in Spanish, English, German and French by strangers who never met.

Honesty about form matters here. Most of the hosts' voices are letters and official papers, not diaries, and they are tagged that way. The Indigenous peoples of the Orinoco and the Andes left no written record of these meetings that we could verify. That includes the paddlers, the porters who stopped at the snow line on Chimborazo, and José de la Cruz of Cumaná, who carried the instruments for five years. They appear here only through Humboldt's pages and one painting, and the entries say so. Bonpland's own botanical journal is a run of numbered plant descriptions that are mostly undated, so much of what we know of him also comes through Humboldt.

Read side by side, the sources show something Humboldt's later books smooth over. He depended on creole scientists who wanted to join him, on colonial officials who were watching him, and on Indigenous guides who knew the rivers and passes far better than he did. When he reached Washington, the first thing a President on the edge of a border quarrel with Spain wanted from him was numbers about New Spain.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian (New Style). Spain, its colonies and the United States all used the Gregorian calendar by 1799. One printed source used here, Delamétherie's 1804 summary of the journey in the Journal de Physique, is dated in the French Republican calendar ('Thermidor an XII', about late July to mid-August 1804). Many of Humboldt's diary pages were written up or recopied days or weeks after the events, so a diary 'date' can mean the day of the event rather than the day of writing. Where only a month or season is known, precision is set to 'month' or 'range'.

eyes.name: Alexander von Humboldt
eyes.role: Prussian naturalist, aged 29–34; former mining official who paid for the expedition himself
eyes.side: Prussia, travelling under a Spanish royal licence
eyes.where: From Cumaná through the Orinoco, Cuba, New Granada, Quito, Lima and New Spain to Philadelphia and Washington
eyes.language: French and German (diaries mostly French; letters to Wilhelm in German)
eyes.authenticity: The American travel diaries (nine bound volumes plus loose sheets) stayed in the family. The Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation bought them for the Berlin State Library in 2013, and they have been digitised and are being edited (Potsdam/BBAW 'edition humboldt'). Many pages were rewritten or added to after the journey. The Personal Narrative (1814–31) is a much later reworking and is treated here as memoir.
eyes.bio: A restless polymath who measured everything: altitude, temperature, magnetism, the blueness of the sky. His diaries mix instrument readings with sharp remarks on colonial abuse, slavery and mission life. He is the hinge between all the other eyes in this chapter, and some of them saw him very differently from how he saw himself.

sources.title: Humboldt Portal, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin (digitised Nachlass and travel diaries)
Universität Potsdam, project 'Die Amerikanischen Reisetagebücher'
Humboldt to Jefferson, 24 May 1804 (Founders Online)
Humboldt to Jefferson, 27 June 1804 (Founders Online)

eyes.name: Aimé Bonpland
eyes.where: At Humboldt's side for the whole journey
eyes.form: journal (numbered botanical descriptions, largely undated); otherwise seen through Humboldt
eyes.authenticity: The 1799–1804 'Journal de botanique' survives in six volumes in the library of the Muséum national d'histoire naturelle, Paris (MSS 1332, 1333, 1334, 2534, 53, 54): 4,528 numbered plant descriptions over 1,318 pages. The entries are numbered, not dated. Bonpland's personal reactions mostly reach us through Humboldt's writing.
eyes.bio: Bonpland collected and described most of the roughly 60,000 specimens, and he nearly died of fever more than once. He is often treated as Humboldt's shadow, but he was the expedition's working botanist. He later went back to South America and spent the rest of his life there.

sources.title: A. Lourteig, 'Aimé Bonpland; sus manuscritos del Museo de París', Bonplandia (1977)

eyes.name: Andrew Ellicott
eyes.role: American surveyor and astronomer, aged 45, US commissioner for the boundary with Spanish Florida
eyes.where: On a vessel in the Florida Keys, then Philadelphia
eyes.vantage_label: same sky, 2,000 km to the north-west
eyes.authenticity: His observation is printed in The Journal of Andrew Ellicott (Philadelphia, 1803), p. 247. He also sent an extract to Jefferson with a letter dated 25 December 1800, which is noted in the Papers of Thomas Jefferson.
eyes.bio: Ellicott had surveyed the boundaries of the District of Columbia and taught Meriwether Lewis how to use survey instruments. On the night of the Leonid storm he was finishing the survey of the US–Spanish boundary along the 31st parallel. His account and Humboldt's are the two best-known eyewitness records of the 1799 storm.

sources.title: Today in Science: Leonid quotations (Ellicott's journal text)
The History Blog, 'Giving Andrew Ellicott his due'
Ellicott to Jefferson, 18 Jan 1801, with editorial note on the 25 Dec letter (Founders Online)

eyes.name: Moravian missionaries at Hopedale, Labrador (and Kapik, through them)
eyes.role: German-speaking Moravian brethren keeping the station diary; Kapik was an Inuit man living at his own camp
eyes.vantage_label: same sky, near the Arctic Circle
eyes.form: mission diary (extracts later printed in the Moravian 'Periodical Accounts')
eyes.authenticity: Known here only through a modern article that quotes the missionaries' report. The exact entry wording and its publication details were not checked. Kapik's own words reach us only through the missionaries, whose purpose was to report conversions. Humboldt himself later noted (Cosmos IV) that the storm frightened people in Labrador and Greenland.
eyes.bio: The Moravians ran small mission stations along the Labrador coast and sent regular diaries home. Their account of 12 November 1799 is valuable because it shows how a man outside both science and the church reacted to the storm. It is also partial: it is a missionary's story about fear leading to conversion.

sources.title: Nunatsiaq News, 'Fireballs and shooting stars'
Humboldt, Cosmos vol. IV (1858), page on the November meteor streams

eyes.name: Indigenous guides and mission communities of the Orinoco (through Humboldt)
eyes.role: Paddlers, pilots and residents of the Franciscan and Capuchin missions; also José de la Cruz of Cumaná, the expedition's servant and instrument-bearer
eyes.side: Indigenous peoples of the Orinoco and Río Negro (among others Maipure, Piaroa, Makiritare/Ye'kuana) and the missions
eyes.where: Atures, Maipures, San Fernando de Atabapo, San Carlos, the Casiquiare, Esmeralda
eyes.vantage_label: hosts and guides (voice preserved only through the traveller)
eyes.form: seen through Humboldt's diaries and later writings (no independent written record verified)
eyes.language: various Indigenous languages; recorded in French, German and Spanish
eyes.authenticity: Flag: these entries are Humboldt's reports of what his hosts did and said, not their own records. The one host-written record mentioned, the mission parish books noting the meteor storm, is known only through Humboldt's Cosmos. We did not verify any surviving Indigenous oral tradition about the 1800 journey.
eyes.bio: Without these pilots the expedition could not have passed the Atures and Maipures rapids or crossed through the Casiquiare. Humboldt depended on their knowledge of rivers, plants and poisons, and rarely named them. Friedrich Weitsch's painting of Chimborazo does put José de la Cruz at the centre, holding the sextant.

sources.title: SPSG: Weitsch, Humboldt and Bonpland at the foot of Chimborazo (on José de la Cruz)
Humboldt, Cosmos vol. IV (1858), p. on mission church books

eyes.name: Pedro Mendinueta y Múzquiz
eyes.authenticity: His reserved letter to minister Pedro Cevallos, dated 19 July 1801, is discussed with archival references in Puig-Samper's article in HiN (Humboldt im Netz).
eyes.bio: The viceroy welcomed the travellers formally and wrote recommendation letters for them to Popayán, Quito and Lima. At the same time he warned Madrid about two highly trained foreigners moving through his realm. His letter is the official side of the welcome.

sources.title: Puig-Samper, '“El favor de la Corte abre todas las puertas”. Aspectos políticos del viaje americano de Alexander von Humboldt', HiN

eyes.name: José Celestino Mutis
eyes.role: Spanish priest-physician, aged 69, director of the Royal Botanical Expedition of New Granada
eyes.side: Spanish Crown / New Granada scientific community
eyes.authenticity: His letters, including one to Humboldt of 21 May 1802 about Caldas, are printed in Mutis's published correspondence and cited in Colombian scholarship (Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia).
eyes.bio: Mutis had spent four decades building a great botanical expedition with a workshop of painters, and he received Humboldt like a son. In print Humboldt praised him generously. In his private diary he grumbled that the old man avoided talking botany. Mutis in turn tried to get his protégé Caldas onto the expedition.

sources.title: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia, Humboldt en la Nueva Granada

eyes.name: Francisco José de Caldas
eyes.role: Creole self-taught astronomer and naturalist from Popayán, aged 33–34
eyes.vantage_label: host scientist who hoped to join
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Mutis are published in his collected correspondence (Cartas de Caldas). Dates used here follow the chronology published by the Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia. That source is inconsistent about whether the first meeting with Humboldt was on 31 December 1801 at Ibarra.
eyes.bio: Caldas had independently worked out how to find altitude from the boiling point of water. He saw in Humboldt the scientific companion he had never had. When Humboldt chose the young nobleman Carlos Montúfar as a travelling companion instead of him, his letters turned bitter. He was later shot by Spanish royalists in 1816 for his part in independence.

sources.title: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia, chronology of Caldas
'Las mediciones barométricas de Humboldt y Caldas en la Nueva Granada'

eyes.name: José de Moraleda y Montero
eyes.role: Spanish naval officer and hydrographer, commander of the corvette Castor
eyes.authenticity: The Castor log (Museo Naval, Madrid, Ms. 612) is described in Puig-Samper's HiN article. Its date range is given as 1803–1804, and its relation to the Callao–Guayaquil passage is not fully clear in our source. Date approximate.
eyes.bio: Moraleda was a careful surveyor of the Chilean coast. In his log he wrote a detailed but partly false biography of Humboldt, saying he had travelled five years with Forster and was still serving the King of Prussia. He also asked whether such a hurried voyage could really be for science. It is the clearest surviving example of the suspicion that followed the travellers.

sources.title: Puig-Samper, HiN article on the political side of the journey

eyes.name: Thomas Jefferson
eyes.role: Third President of the United States, aged 61
eyes.authenticity: His letters survive as press copies in the Library of Congress and are published in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson (Founders Online).
eyes.bio: Jefferson had just completed the Louisiana Purchase and sent Lewis and Clark west, and he faced a disputed border with Spain. Humboldt arrived with fresh data from New Spain. The friendship that followed lasted by letter for the rest of Jefferson's life.

sources.title: Jefferson to Humboldt, 28 May 1804
Jefferson to Humboldt, 9 June 1804
Monticello: Alexander von Humboldt (Silhouette)

eyes.name: Charles Willson Peale
eyes.role: Painter, naturalist and museum keeper of Philadelphia, aged 63
eyes.authenticity: Peale's diary of the 1804 journey is published in The Selected Papers of Charles Willson Peale and His Family. Details here follow G. Casper's study 'A Young Man from Ultima Thule…' and the Monticello and Smithsonian pages.
eyes.bio: Peale ran America's first great natural-history museum and led the small party that took Humboldt, Bonpland and Montúfar to Washington. He cut a silhouette of Humboldt, painted his portrait, and recorded the President's dinner. He wrote as a fellow collector, delighted to have such a guest.

sources.title: G. Casper, 'A Young Man from Ultima Thule Visits Jefferson'
Smithsonian American Art Museum: Peale's portrait of Humboldt

eyes.name: Albert Gallatin
eyes.role: US Secretary of the Treasury, aged 43, Swiss-born
eyes.authenticity: His letter to his wife Hannah of 6 June 1804 is cited from the Gallatin papers in Casper's study. Wording not checked against the manuscript.
eyes.bio: Gallatin was a French-speaking Genevan with a passion for maps and statistics, and he was the cabinet member most eager to mine Humboldt's data on New Spain. His private letter gives a quick, unguarded first impression.

sources.title: G. Casper, 'A Young Man from Ultima Thule Visits Jefferson'

entries.place: A Coruña, aboard the corvette Pizarro
entries.headline: Sailing past a British blockade with forty-two instruments
entries.digest: Humboldt and Bonpland sailed from A Coruña on the Spanish mail corvette Pizarro, slipping past British warships watching the port. Humboldt's diary for the Spain-to-Cumaná leg begins a habit he kept for five years of logging readings several times a day. Here they were sea temperature, sky colour and his instruments. He carried a royal licence wider than any foreign scientist had held in Spanish America.
entries.source_note: Departure date in Lourteig's summary of Bonpland's MS 211; diary volume 'Voyage d'Espagne aux Canaries et à Cumaná' (Tagebücher der Amerikanischen Reise I, ed. Leitner & Götz).

entries.headline: Landfall at Cumaná: running about like madmen among plants
entries.digest: After an outbreak of fever on board pushed the Pizarro to change course, they came ashore at Cumaná. In a letter to Wilhelm dated the same day, as usually cited, Humboldt describes himself and Bonpland as dizzy with wonder. They ran from tree to tree, picking up one thing and dropping it for the next, unable to settle on anything for days. Palms, flamingos and crabs all crowd into the letter.
entries.source_note: Letter to Wilhelm von Humboldt, Cumaná, 16 July 1799 (published in Humboldt's Briefe aus Amerika 1799–1804, ed. Moheit). Arrival date per standard chronology and Delamétherie (1804). Exact letter date not re-checked online.

entries.headline: Plant number one: the botanical journal begins
entries.digest: Bonpland's first journal volume (MS 1332) holds descriptions 1 to 690, running from Tenerife through the coast of Venezuela. Each plant got a number and a careful Latin description. Where he could not name the species he left a gap, and the botanist Kunth filled those gaps decades later in Paris. It is a working record with almost no personal comment, and it shows how much of the expedition's science was his.
entries.source_note: Lourteig, Bonplandia (1977), appendix listing MSS 1332–54. Entries are numbered, not dated; date range inferred from the volume's coverage.

entries.headline: Thousands of fire-balls over Cumaná until dawn
entries.digest: From about half past two in the morning the eastern sky over Cumaná filled with meteors. There were thousands of fire-balls and falling stars, some leaving glowing trails for several seconds. Humboldt timed and measured them, and noticed they all seemed to come from one point. Local fishermen said it had started around one o'clock. An old resident recalled that lights like these had come before the great earthquakes of 1766, and that worried a town still shaken by a quake on 4 November.
entries.source_note: Personal Narrative (written later, from the diary); Cosmos IV (1858) p. on November streams; summary of Bonpland's observations in Clarke, Hundred Wonders of the World (e-rara).

entries.headline: Bonpland, up for cool air, sees the sky ignite first
entries.digest: Bonpland had got up to enjoy the cool night air on the gallery and was the first to see the meteors. He reported that from the start there was no patch of sky three moons wide that was free of falling stars and fire-balls. Some of the largest burst without sparks and left broad glowing streaks. His observations reach us only through Humboldt's account.
entries.source_note: Flag: through Humboldt. Bonpland's description as relayed in Humboldt's Personal Narrative and quoted in Clarke (e-rara page).

entries.place: Aboard a vessel in the Florida Keys
entries.headline: Woken at two: the whole sky full of rockets
entries.digest: Ellicott was woken around two in the morning to a sky full of meteors streaking in every direction. He called the sight grand and awful, and worried that some might land on the ship. The display lasted until daylight washed it out. He later learned it had been seen across much of the West Indies and as far north as St. Marys, Georgia. Neither he nor Humboldt yet knew that the other had been watching.
entries.quote: the whole heavens appeared as if illuminated with skyrockets
entries.source_note: The Journal of Andrew Ellicott (Philadelphia, 1803), p. 247, as quoted by Today in Science and The History Blog.

entries.headline: Kapik runs to the mission in terror
entries.digest: At Hopedale the missionaries recorded that Kapik, an Inuk who had opposed their preaching and lived at his own camp, was almost out of his mind with fear at the falling stars. He ran to the station, woke everyone, and urged them to turn to God. The missionaries say he became a Christian soon after. Kapik's own reasons are only as the missionaries told them.
entries.source_note: Moravian report as quoted in Nunatsiaq News, 'Fireballs and shooting stars'; original Periodical Accounts entry not checked. Humboldt, Cosmos IV, confirms reports from Labrador and Greenland.

entries.headline: First diary volume closes as they sail west
entries.digest: Humboldt's first diary volume, the Cumaná book, ends here. He and Bonpland left by sea for La Guaira and Caracas carrying their first crates of plants, and the second volume opens with Caracas. Behind them were the cave of the oil-birds at Caripe, an earthquake and the meteor storm. The man who had arrived 'like a fool' among the plants was now running a full programme of measurements.
entries.source_note: Volume dates per U. Leitner's survey of the diaries (Cumaná 3.6.–18.11.1799; Caracas 18.11.1799 onward). Sailing day per standard chronology.

entries.headline: Fiery rays again: the people fear the world's end
entries.digest: Two months later the Hopedale diarists saw what they called immense fiery rays and balls in the night sky, probably an aurora or fireballs. They wrote that the Inuit took the lights as a sign that the world was about to end. The missionaries did not contradict them and preached repentance instead. These are two winter nights in one mission diary, and both times the sky became an argument for conversion.
entries.source_note: Nunatsiaq News article ('a few months later', 14 January). Year inferred as 1800; original entry not checked.

entries.place: Caracas, heading south into the Llanos
entries.headline: Into the Llanos, toward the Orinoco
entries.digest: Humboldt and Bonpland left Caracas, crossed the Aragua valleys around Lake Valencia and headed out onto the burning flat Llanos. At Calabozo they had local men drive horses into a pool so they could study electric eels, which cost several horses and left the travellers stunned and aching. The diaries for this leg mix eel experiments with notes on cattle ranches and enslaved labour.
entries.source_note: Delamétherie, 'Short Account…' (1804), February 1800 departure; eel episode per diaries and Personal Narrative. Exact day not verified.

entries.headline: Pilots haul the canoe through the great rapids
entries.digest: At the Atures and Maipures rapids, mission pilots unloaded the canoe and dragged it over the rocks while the travellers walked around. Humboldt was told of a burial cave of the Atures people, who had vanished, and of a parrot at Maipures that was said to speak words of their language that no one living understood. The parrot story comes only from Humboldt, who heard it from local informants. It survives as his image of a culture lost to epidemics and the missions.
entries.source_note: Flag: seen through Humboldt (Personal Narrative; Ansichten der Natur). Month approximate; Delamétherie (1804) confirms the passage of the Atures and Maipures cataracts.

entries.place: Missions of the upper Orinoco and Río Negro
entries.headline: Parish books on the river record the meteor night
entries.digest: In the forest missions toward the Río Negro, Humboldt found that missionaries had seen the 'enormous fall of meteors' of November 1799. Some had written it into their parish books. It is a rare host-written trace of the storm from deep in the interior, and we know of it only because Humboldt mentions it. On the same stretch, Indigenous paddlers took the canoe through the Casiquiare, the natural canal linking the Orinoco and Amazon systems, which they already knew well and Europeans doubted.
entries.source_note: Humboldt, Cosmos IV (1858) page on November streams (church books); Casiquiare passage per Delamétherie (1804). Month approximate.

entries.headline: At the edge of the map, watching curare made
entries.digest: At Esmeralda, the farthest mission upriver, Humboldt watched a local expert prepare curare poison from vines. He was impressed by the man's chemical skill and calm confidence, and wrote with sympathy about him. Insects, hunger and damp had nearly ruined their instruments and collections. This was the turning point, and from here they let the river carry them back down toward Angostura.
entries.source_note: Esmeralda per Delamétherie (1804) 'Esmeraldo'; curare episode per Personal Narrative. Day not verified.

entries.place: Havana and the interior of Cuba
entries.headline: Cuba diary: sugar, slavery and the island's numbers
entries.digest: Humboldt's Cuba diary, 'Isle de Cube. Antilles en général', covers his first stay on the island. That includes an inland excursion in January and February and a trip south to Batabanó and Trinidad in early March. He gathered population and sugar statistics and saw the slave economy close up, which became the basis of his later outspoken attack on slavery. This was the first diary fragment published in the new digital edition, in 2017.
entries.source_note: U. Leitner's survey of the diaries (Kuba I, 29.12.1800–15.3.1801).

entries.headline: A grand welcome, and a sour private note on Mutis
entries.digest: Coming up from the Magdalena after weeks at Honda, where Bonpland had been sick with fever, the travellers were met outside the capital by a formal delegation and given a house next to Mutis's. Publicly Humboldt praised Mutis as a kindly, toothless old man who had built a great scientific enterprise almost alone, and who opened his herbarium freely. In the private diary he complained that Mutis avoided talking about botany.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia, Humboldt en la Nueva Granada (gives entry on 15 July; other accounts give early July).

entries.headline: Viceroy's confidential letter: welcome, but watch them
entries.digest: A few days after the travellers arrived, the viceroy wrote privately to minister Cevallos in Madrid and enclosed a copy of their passport. He admitted their conduct gave no grounds for suspicion, but he was uneasy about two such well-trained foreigners. He mentioned a warning from the governor of Cartagena and reported that he had told other authorities to watch their movements and act if needed. The same official wrote them warm letters of recommendation for the road south.
entries.source_note: Carta reservada, Mendinueta to Pedro Cevallos, 19 July 1801, discussed in Puig-Samper, HiN (hin-online.de article 284).

entries.headline: A provincial astronomer introduces himself to Mutis
entries.digest: Caldas opened his correspondence with Mutis with a long letter telling his life story. He described how he had taught himself astronomy and built instruments from scratch in a provincial town. A week later he set out for Quito on a family lawsuit, without yet knowing that Humboldt would soon pass that way.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia, chronology of Caldas (5 Aug 1801 letter; 11 Aug departure).

entries.headline: Christmas in Pasto after the worst road yet
entries.digest: Writing to Wilhelm from Pasto, Humboldt described the mule track over the páramos from Popayán as more horrible than anything he could put into words. They waded through mud and slept in rain, and Indigenous carriers took loads, and sometimes travellers, on their backs. Bonpland was worn out. Ahead lay Ibarra and Quito.
entries.source_note: Letter to Wilhelm from Pasto, Christmas 1801, per Nature's Interpreter ch. 6 (Lutterworth extract). Exact date not given there.

entries.headline: Caldas rides north to meet his hero
entries.digest: Hearing that Humboldt was coming south, Caldas left Quito and met him at Ibarra. Writing about it afterwards, he called it the happiest moment a lover of science could hope for. He showed Humboldt his method of finding altitude from the boiling point of water, and Humboldt took it seriously. Caldas began to hope he might travel on with the expedition.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia chronology (31 Dec 1801; source itself inconsistent on the first meeting).

entries.headline: Arrival in Quito, a city still rebuilding
entries.digest: Humboldt reached Quito, where he would stay eight or nine months as a guest of the Montúfar family. The 1797 earthquake that had killed tens of thousands in the province was still on everyone's mind, yet Quito society struck him as lively and pleasure-loving. Over the following months he climbed Pichincha more than once and looked into its crater.
entries.source_note: Delamétherie, 'Short Account of Travels between the Tropics' (1804), Bern digital edition.

entries.headline: Pleading with Mutis to let him join Humboldt
entries.digest: Caldas wrote to Mutis about his hope of joining the expedition. Elsewhere he recalled a day in early April 1802 with Humboldt as one he would never forget. Mutis backed him, offered to pay his costs, and wrote to recommend him. Caldas was sure his chance had come.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia, Humboldt en la Nueva Granada (Caldas to Mutis, 6 April 1802) and Caldas chronology (3 April recollection).

entries.headline: Refused: Caldas pours out his grievance
entries.digest: Humboldt said no. He chose the young aristocrat Carlos Montúfar as his companion, and Caldas, poor and creole, felt passed over. In a letter to Mutis he vented his complaints about Humboldt's character and choices. The two men still exchanged measurements politely, but the hurt is plain in the letter.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia, chronology of Caldas (21 April 1802).

entries.headline: Mutis writes to Humboldt on Caldas's behalf
entries.digest: Mutis wrote to Humboldt in Quito as part of the exchange over Caldas. He was trying to keep the goodwill of a famous visitor while finding a place for his protégé. When Humboldt's refusal stood, Mutis took Caldas into the royal Botanical Expedition and sent him to study cinchona (quina) in the Quito region. In practice the old man gave Caldas the scientific career Humboldt would not.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia (Mutis to Humboldt, 21 May 1802; outcome per Caldas chronology). Letter content summarised from secondary account.

entries.headline: Higher than anyone recorded, short of the summit
entries.digest: With Bonpland and Montúfar, Humboldt climbed the ridge of Chimborazo, then thought to be the world's highest mountain. The Indigenous porters stopped at the snow line and would go no farther. Above it the men edged along a narrow ridge in thin air, with nosebleeds, bleeding gums and nausea, until a crevasse stopped them at about 3,036 toises (around 5,900 m by his reckoning). Humboldt treated the altitude sickness as a scientific finding and began sketching the zones of plant life up the mountain.
entries.source_note: Delamétherie (1804) for date and height; DHM journal on the diary account and symptoms.

entries.headline: Bleeding at the nose, still collecting
entries.digest: On the climb Bonpland had nosebleeds like the others, and he went on noting the last plants and lichens below the snow. What he saw on the climb survives only through Humboldt's account. His numbered journal descriptions are not dated, so they cannot be pinned to the day. Back in Europe, the painter Weitsch showed him seated under a tent with a book at the mountain's foot.
entries.source_note: Flag: through Humboldt (DHM journal summary of the diary). Weitsch painting per SPSG.

entries.headline: The porters who stopped at the snow
entries.digest: The Indigenous carriers of the Chimborazo party refused to go above the snow line, and the Europeans went on alone. We know of them only as figures in Humboldt's account, and their reasons are not recorded. A related figure, José de la Cruz of Cumaná, had served the expedition since 1799 as servant and instrument-bearer. In Weitsch's painting he stands at the centre handing Humboldt the sextant, and he is left out of its title.
entries.source_note: Flag: seen through Humboldt and a European painting. DHM journal; SPSG page on Weitsch (José de la Cruz). This eye's label covers Indigenous and local helpers across the journey.

entries.headline: Timing Mercury's crossing of the Sun at Callao
entries.digest: At the port of Callao, Humboldt observed the transit of Mercury across the Sun and used it to fix the longitude of Lima. Getting that longitude right was the point. Correcting the maps of Spanish America with exact positions was one of his main goals. In the same weeks he measured the cold coastal current that would later bear his name.
entries.source_note: Nature's Interpreter ch. 6 (Lutterworth extract); Delamétherie (1804).

entries.headline: Same transit, watched from the Andes
entries.digest: Now working for Mutis's Botanical Expedition, Caldas watched the same transit of Mercury from Otavalo in the northern Andes, roughly 1,400 km north of Humboldt. Unlike Humboldt, he had no royal licence or European instrument makers, but he was taking part in the same kind of measurement. That autumn he also climbed Imbabura and laid out a survey baseline near Lake San Pablo.
entries.source_note: Sociedad Geográfica de Colombia chronology (Mercury transit from Otavalo, late 1802). Day inferred from the date of the transit.

entries.headline: To Wilhelm: the story of Chimborazo
entries.digest: From Lima Humboldt wrote his brother a long letter full of the drama of the Andes. He described the climb on Chimborazo, the thin air and the height they reached, and set out plans for Mexico. The letter was also aimed at learned Europe, which had heard little from him in many months.
entries.source_note: Letter of 25 Nov 1802 cited in Brewminate, 'Nature, politics and the story of Mt Chimborazo in 1802'. Place (Lima) per standard chronology.

entries.headline: A naval log builds a suspect's dossier
entries.digest: The travellers sailed north from Callao toward Guayaquil 'by superior order'. Around this time Commander Moraleda wrote a long, partly invented account of Humboldt in his log: five years of travel with Forster, still in the King of Prussia's service, and a voyage too rushed to be honest science. It is the clearest example of the suspicion that the viceroys' polite letters covered up.
entries.source_note: Castor log, Museo Naval Madrid Ms. 612, as described in Puig-Samper (HiN). Exact entry date not established; departure from Callao in December 1802.

entries.headline: Landfall in New Spain, a letter to the viceroy
entries.digest: Humboldt landed at Acapulco and wrote that same day to the new viceroy, José de Iturrigaray, to announce himself. He also took measurements of the port. Four days later the party began the climb up to the capital.
entries.source_note: Fuentes Humanísticas (UAM) article on Humboldt in Mexico.

entries.headline: Into Mexico City at dusk
entries.digest: At dusk the travellers entered Mexico City and took rooms in calle San Agustín. Humboldt's Mexico City diary runs from the next day to January 1804. Within days the viceroy opened the colonial archives to him. He examined at the School of Mines and gathered the statistics that became his Political Essay on New Spain.
entries.source_note: Fuentes Humanísticas (UAM) article (arrival 11 April; diary 12.4.1803–20.1.1804; audience 15 April).

entries.headline: A thank-you to the viceroy in tables
entries.digest: Before leaving, Humboldt gave Viceroy Iturrigaray his 'Tablas geográficas y políticas' of New Spain with a covering letter. The tables summarised population, mines, revenue and geography. He was paying back his hosts in the currency he valued most, data. Copies of that kind of data were exactly what Washington would soon ask him for.
entries.source_note: Fuentes Humanísticas (UAM) article (letter of 3 January 1804).

entries.headline: Fresh off the ship, writing to Jefferson
entries.digest: The day after landing from Havana on the Concepción, after a storm off Georgia that he thought might kill them, Humboldt wrote to Jefferson in French. He praised the President's writings and his liberal ideas, summarised five years of travel, and boasted of the height reached on Chimborazo. He added mammoth teeth from the Andes to tempt a fellow fossil enthusiast. He wrote that he had come to see a people who understood the value of liberty.
entries.source_note: Humboldt to Jefferson, 24 May 1804, Founders Online 01-43-02-0369; arrival 23 May per Casper.

entries.headline: The President replies: little here but a welcome
entries.digest: Jefferson answered the morning after Humboldt's letter reached him. He welcomed the traveller's safe return and called the lands he had seen the least known and most interesting. He apologised that the raw new capital offered little worth seeing apart from a warm welcome. He added a line of hope about the improved condition of humankind in the New World.
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Humboldt, 28 May 1804, Founders Online 01-43-02-0389.

entries.headline: Peale's party reaches the President's House
entries.digest: Peale led a small party from Philadelphia, made up of Humboldt, Bonpland, Montúfar and the scholars Nicholas Collin and Anthony Fothergill, and recorded the journey in his diary. They reached Washington on 1 June. The next morning Humboldt paid his first formal call on Jefferson. Peale enjoyed playing guide to the most famous traveller alive.
entries.source_note: Monticello, 'Alexander von Humboldt (Silhouette)'; Casper, 'A Young Man from Ultima Thule' (arrival 1 June, visit 2 June).

entries.headline: Dinner with no toasts and no politics
entries.digest: Peale described the President's dinner for Humboldt, Bonpland, Montúfar and the Philadelphia visitors as very elegant. No toasts were given and politics was not discussed. The table talked about natural history, improvements in daily life, and the customs of different nations. To Peale, the evening showed the Republic he believed in, plain and run on learning.
entries.source_note: Peale's diary as cited in Casper, 'A Young Man from Ultima Thule…'.

entries.headline: The botanist at the President's table
entries.digest: Bonpland sat at Jefferson's dinner alongside Humboldt and Montúfar. In American accounts he is a name on the guest list rather than a voice. The cases of plants he had described in South America were still stuck in Philadelphia and Havana. Of the three companions who had stood together on Chimborazo, only Humboldt is quoted by the American witnesses.
entries.source_note: Flag: presence only, per Peale's diary as cited by Casper.

entries.headline: Two hours with Humboldt worth two years
entries.digest: The Treasury Secretary wrote to his wife that he had learned more from Humboldt in two hours than he had read or heard in the previous two years. Gallatin loved maps and statistics, and Humboldt had both for New Spain, including the northern borderlands now facing the United States. The letter catches a powerful official's quick, excited first impression.
entries.source_note: Gallatin to Hannah Gallatin, 6 June 1804, as cited in Casper.

entries.headline: A President's questions about the Spanish border
entries.digest: Jefferson sent Humboldt a precise question. Between the boundary Spain claimed for Louisiana, the Sabine River, and the one the United States claimed, the Rio Grande ('North River'), how many white, Indigenous and Black inhabitants lived, and were there any mines? The new purchase had a disputed western edge, and Humboldt had just come from the archives of Mexico City. Humboldt's undated reply followed.
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Humboldt, 9 June 1804, Founders Online 01-43-02-0455.

entries.headline: Praising the Republic, condemning its slavery
entries.digest: Writing to William Thornton, architect of the Capitol, Humboldt criticised slavery in the United States. It was the same institution he had seen at work on the sugar estates of Cuba. Admiring the country's free institutions did not stop him from naming this contradiction in them, even to his hosts.
entries.source_note: Casper, 'A Young Man from Ultima Thule…' (letter to Thornton, 20 June 1804).

entries.headline: A farewell letter to Jefferson
entries.digest: With his collections loaded and a ship for France waiting, Humboldt sent Jefferson a farewell letter. He was leaving after about six weeks in the United States. The friendship continued by letter for two more decades, with Humboldt sending volumes of his Voyage and Jefferson reading them closely.
entries.source_note: Founders Online 01-43-02-0552 (title and date); Casper. Text not fetched.

entries.headline: Leaving America, the five years in two pages
entries.digest: On the day he left, Humboldt sent the Philadelphia scholar John Vaughan an overview of the whole expedition to be translated and published. It ran from Cumaná and the Orinoco to Quito, Chimborazo, Lima and Mexico. A version soon appeared in Europe as the 'Short Account of Travels between the Tropics'. He reached Bordeaux in August 1804.
entries.source_note: Casper (30 June 1804, overview to Vaughan); Delamétherie, 'Short Account…' (Thermidor an XII / 1804), Bern digital edition.

entries.headline: Sending the meteor night to Jefferson
entries.digest: Back in Philadelphia, Ellicott wrote to Jefferson and enclosed an extract from his journal describing the meteors he had seen at sea off Florida on 12 November 1799. He was offering it as data, for the American Philosophical Society circle in which Jefferson was a leading figure. Three and a half years later Jefferson would be welcoming Humboldt, who had watched the same sky from Cumaná.
entries.source_note: Editorial note to Ellicott to Jefferson, 18 Jan 1801 (Founders Online 01-32-02-0343), mentioning a letter of 25 December with the journal extract. Year inferred as 1800 from the volume's date range.

entries.headline: A portrait and a silhouette for the museum
entries.digest: Peale cut a paper silhouette of Humboldt at his museum and gave Jefferson a set of silhouettes. He also painted Humboldt's portrait just before the traveller returned to Europe, for his gallery of eminent figures. Writing to his father-in-law, he said Humboldt's conversation had repaid all the cost and trouble of the journey. He called Humboldt the most extraordinary traveller he had met.
entries.source_note: Smithsonian American Art Museum page on Peale's portrait (1804); Monticello silhouette page. Letter date not given.

convergences.label: The Leonid meteor storm
convergences.note: The same storm was seen from four places. Humboldt measured it as a natural philosopher and noticed the meteors' common origin point. Bonpland simply saw it first. Ellicott, at sea, felt it as grand and awful and feared for his ship. At Hopedale it became a story of terror and conversion. Humboldt later put these and others, including the Orinoco parish books, Greenland and Weimar, into Cosmos, which helped establish that meteor showers return periodically.

convergences.label: Spring 1800 on the Orinoco and Casiquiare
convergences.note: The traveller's diary and the hosts' world overlap here, but the hosts are heard only through him. Pilots, missionaries and a curare maker supplied the knowledge, including the friars' own written record of the meteor night, and Humboldt supplied the measurements.

convergences.label: Bogotá: the welcome and the watch
convergences.note: The same week has three versions. There was a public welcome with a house beside Mutis. Humboldt privately complained about his host. And the viceroy sent a confidential letter warning Madrid about the two foreigners.

convergences.label: Quito, spring 1802: who gets to travel with Humboldt
convergences.note: Caldas pleaded, Mutis lobbied and offered to pay, and Humboldt chose the aristocrat Montúfar. The creole scientist's letters show the cost of being the host, not the guest.

convergences.label: Chimborazo
convergences.note: Three Europeans and a creole climbed into thin air while the Indigenous porters stayed at the snow line. Humboldt's diary gives the science and the symptoms. The others are known only through his pages and Weitsch's painting.

convergences.label: Transit of Mercury
convergences.note: The man who was refused and the man who refused him timed the same planet crossing the Sun on the same day, about 1,400 km apart, one at Callao and one at Otavalo.

convergences.label: Washington, 1–9 June 1804
convergences.note: There were elegant dinners with no politics, by Peale's account. Meanwhile Gallatin was dazzled and Jefferson was quietly drafting questions about the Louisiana border. The welcome was warm and it was also useful to the government.

ties.note: Companions for the entire five years, from A Coruña to Washington.
Met at Ibarra at the turn of 1801–02 and exchanged measurements in Quito. Humboldt turned down Caldas's wish to join the expedition.
Mutis championed Caldas and, after Humboldt's refusal, took him into the Botanical Expedition.
Guest and host in Bogotá in 1801. Humboldt praised him in public and was more critical in private.
The viceroy recommended him to other officials and also had him watched.
The naval log describes Humboldt with suspicion and partly false details.
Met in Washington in June 1804 and wrote to each other for two decades afterwards.
Peale took him to Washington, painted his portrait and cut his silhouette.
Gallatin was dazzled by Humboldt's data on New Spain.
Ellicott sent Jefferson his journal extract on the meteor storm. They were close colleagues in the American Philosophical Society circle.
They never met, but their accounts of 12 November 1799 became the two classic records of the storm.
Humboldt later cited reports from Labrador and Greenland in Cosmos when he compared observations of the storm.
His pilots, hosts and informants. Their knowledge reached Europe only under his name.

threads_out.note: The Endeavour sailed in 1768 partly to observe the 1769 transit of Venus, the same transit Chappe observed in California and that Humboldt mentioned to Jefferson. Humboldt's own longitudes rested on a transit of Mercury at Callao in 1802. His early mentor Georg Forster had sailed on Cook's next voyage, and Moraleda's log wrongly claimed Humboldt had travelled with Forster for five years.

Humboldt arrived in Washington three weeks after Lewis and Clark set off up the Missouri. Jefferson immediately asked him about the disputed western border of Louisiana. Ellicott had trained Lewis in surveying, and Peale's museum later displayed specimens from the expedition.

Humboldt's Vues des Cordillères (1810–13) and his later Examen critique on Columbus re-examined the encounter of 1492 and the Indigenous civilisations that followed it. They drew directly on what he learned in Mexico and the Andes.
In 1817, the year after Tambora's 'year without a summer', Humboldt published his paper on isotherms, a way of mapping climate built from the temperature readings he had taken across the Americas.

Humboldt and Bonpland met in revolutionary Paris in 1798 while looking for a voyage, and they returned to Napoleonic Paris in August 1804 to publish. Delamétherie's first account of the journey is dated in the Republican calendar.
